overview: Bremen was a free trading city on the Weser. The imported 1715 to 1878 interval is incomplete: French rule interrupted independence, and the city continued afterward. The small outline also omits its later port at Bremerhaven.

periods.title: A free city in a changing Europe
periods.summary: Bremen defended its autonomy through the final century of the Holy Roman Empire.

periods.title: Restoration and federal membership
periods.summary: The restored city joined successive German political unions and developed an overseas port.

sections.title: Rights, rulers and a city’s printed words

items.text: Bremen’s imperial recognition as a free city dated to 1646, before this entry begins. A settlement at Stade in 1741 resolved remaining disputes with neighboring Hanover over its status. Even a trading republic needed treaties: ships and merchants benefited when the city could defend its right to govern itself.

In 1810 the Hanseatic cities were annexed to Napoleon’s empire, and Bremen became the center of the Department of the Weser Mouths. Its restored government later joined the German Confederation in 1815. This interruption matters: a continuously colored map shape does not mean the same government remained in charge throughout.

The revolution of 1848 brought a parliamentary election in which male citizens aged twenty-five and over could, in principle, vote on equal terms. A new constitution followed in 1849, giving the elected assembly legislative powers alongside the Senate. This was an expansion of participation, but citizenship, age and sex still limited it.

The gains did not all last. Opponents within Bremen’s leadership sought support from the restored German Confederation, and in 1854 a revised constitution reversed equal voting rights among citizens and strengthened the Senate. The city’s own modern account treats this as a rollback, rather than a smooth march toward democracy.

Writing sample: “Sammlung der Verordnungen und Proclame” means “Collection of ordinances and proclamations.” These German words begin the title of the Senate’s printed legal series, including its 1849 volume preserved by Bremen’s State and University Library. The old spelling Proclame survives in the title; publication date and dates of individual orders must be checked separately.

sections.title: A port for journeys across the Atlantic

items.text: The Weser’s silting made access for seagoing ships a persistent problem. In 1827 Bremen acquired land from Hanover near the river mouth and began building Bremerhaven. This separate port gave the city an outlet nearer the open sea, changing the geography of a state whose interests stretched well beyond its old streets.

Bremerhaven’s emigrants’ house opened in April 1850 for people waiting to sail overseas. It could lodge up to 2,000 people, while a steam-equipped kitchen could prepare 3,500 portions. Sailors and dockworkers also ate there. Those figures describe its capacity, but they convey the scale of feeding a temporary community.

The emigrants’ house had nine large dormitories arranged rather like a ship’s between-decks accommodation, with bunks intended for three or four people. Washing rooms stood before the dormitories, and medical rooms offered care. Travel involved waiting, sharing space and staying healthy before passengers had even crossed the ocean.

sections.title: Households, school and a portrait before cameras

items.text: Bremen’s territory also contained rural households. The surviving Mittelsbüren farmhouse was built in 1586 or 1587 and remained part of village life for centuries. Its hall and open Flett hearth illustrate a setting where cooking and warmth centered on a fire; separate living, sleeping and kitchen areas were later additions.

When Bremen senator Johann Smidt visited Paris in 1811, he tried a fashionable mechanical portrait process. A device helped trace his profile, after which an engraver made reduced prints. Smidt complained that the result did not look like him and tried another artist in 1814. Disappointing portraits certainly existed before awkward photographs.

Bremen introduced state compulsory schooling in 1844. The School Museum studies that change through teaching equipment, schoolbooks, photographs and written records. These sources make it possible to investigate how rules about attendance became part of childhood, rather than assuming every child had always received the same education.

The water tower completed on the Stadtwerder in 1873 looks like a brick castle, but its corner turrets had practical jobs. Two served as steam-engine chimneys, one contained stairs, and another held the rising and falling water pipes. The 47-meter structure wrapped water-supply machinery in an unusually grand architectural coat.

ending.text: Bremen joined the North German Confederation in 1867 and became a constituent state of the German Empire in 1871, surrendering its separate foreign-policy role. The city continued beyond 1878; the imported endpoint marks no destruction or disappearance of its people.
